content: Rudbeckia hirta, commonly known as Black-eyed Susan, Blackiehead, Brown Betty, Brown Daisy, Brown-eyed Susan, Gloriosa Daisy, Golden Jerusalem, Poorland Daisy, Yellow Daisy, or Yellow Ox-eye Daisy, is a flowering plant belonging to the family Asteraceae. This plant is typically an upright annual, though it can sometimes be biennial or perennial. It is native to most regions of North America. The plant is notable for its characteristic appearance, with yellow ray florets encircling a brown, domed center composed of disc florets. In some cases, the plant may also exhibit purple coloration on the sides. Rudbeckia hirta can grow to a height of 1 to 2 meters. These leaves are covered with coarse hair. The plant blooms between June and August, producing inflorescences that are typically 10 to 15 cm in diameter, though some cultivated varieties can reach up to 30 cm. There are four recognized varieties of Rudbeckia hirta: 1. Rudbeckia hirta var. angustifolia: Found in the southeastern United States, ranging from South Carolina to Texas. 2. Rudbeckia hirta var. floridana: Endemic to Florida. 3. Rudbeckia hirta var. hirta: Found in the northeastern United States, from Maine to Alabama. 4. Rudbeckia hirta var. pulcherrima: Widespread across most of North America, from Newfoundland to British Columbia, and extending south to Alabama and New Mexico. It has also been naturalized in regions from Washington to California. In 1918, Black-eyed Susan was officially designated as the state Floral Emblem of Maryland. Numerous cultivars of this plant have been developed for ornamental garden use. Popular cultivars include 'Double Gold,' 'Indian Summer,' and 'Marmalade.' The roots of Rudbeckia hirta, though not its seedheads, have been used medicinally in ways similar to the related plant Echinacea purpurea. The plant has astringent properties and can be prepared as a warm infusion for use as a wash to treat sores and swellings. The Ojibwe people traditionally used the plant as a poultice for snake bites and prepared an infusion to treat colds and intestinal worms in children. Additionally, the plant has diuretic properties and was used by the Menominee and Potawatomi tribes. Juice extracted from the roots was historically used as ear drops to alleviate earaches. Rudbeckia hirta contains anthocyanins, which are pigments with potential biological activity.
